nameStory: The Atlantic salmon gets its name from being the salmon of the Atlantic Ocean, as opposed to the many salmon species found in the Pacific. The word 'salmon' comes from the Latin 'salmo,' which likely derives from 'salire' meaning 'to leap' - a perfect description of these incredible fish that leap up waterfalls and rapids to reach their spawning grounds.
description: Atlantic salmon are sleek, powerful fish that can grow up to 3 feet long, making them the third largest member of the salmon and trout family. These amazing fish are born in freshwater streams, swim out to the ocean to grow and mature, then return to their birth rivers to spawn. Unlike their Pacific cousins, Atlantic salmon can survive spawning and make this incredible journey multiple times in their lives, though most only do it once.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, torpedo-shaped body built for powerful swimming with a slightly compressed (flattened from side to side) profile that feels firm and muscular when handled

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Silver sides with a darker back when in the ocean; spawning adults develop darker colors with reddish hues and may feel slightly rough to the touch from breeding changes

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Small adipose fin (a fleshy, rayless fin) between the dorsal fin and tail - feels like a soft bump when touched; tail fin is only slightly forked in adults

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth that extends to or slightly past the eye when closed; inside of mouth is white or pale (unlike some trout species with darker mouths)

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach up to 3 feet in length and feel surprisingly heavy - much larger than most other New England salmonids when fully grown

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in cold, clear rivers and streams connected to the ocean; young fish prefer areas with gravel bottoms that feel rough underfoot and have good water flow

habitat: Atlantic salmon are found in cold, clear rivers and streams that flow into the Atlantic Ocean throughout New England. They prefer waters with gravel or rocky bottoms, good oxygen levels, and cool temperatures year-round. Young salmon need shallow areas with rifles and pools, while adults use deeper sections during their spawning runs.

seasonality.spring: Adult salmon begin entering rivers from the ocean in late spring, appearing bright silver and in peak condition. This is when you're most likely to spot large, healthy-looking fish in river mouths and lower river sections.
seasonality.summer: Spawning runs continue through summer, with fish moving upstream to reach their natal waters. Fish may show some darkening of color as they spend more time in freshwater.
seasonality.fall: Peak spawning season when adults develop their most dramatic color changes, becoming darker with reddish tones. This is the best time to observe their spawning behavior in shallow gravel areas.
seasonality.winter: Young salmon remain in streams through winter, while surviving spawning adults may return to the ocean. Ice-free areas may reveal small parr (juvenile salmon) with distinctive dark vertical bars on their sides.

funFact: Atlantic salmon are like the ultimate GPS system - they can return to the exact same gravel bed where they were born after spending years roaming thousands of miles in the ocean, navigating by smell, magnetic fields, and even the position of the sun!
confusionNotes: Atlantic salmon are most easily confused with large brown trout, but salmon have a more streamlined body shape and their tail fin connects to the body with a narrower 'wrist' area - imagine the difference between a torpedo (salmon) and a football (trout). Remember: salmon are built for ocean travel, trout for river life.
contextualKnowledge: Most 'Atlantic salmon' you see in stores or restaurants are actually farm-raised fish that have never seen the ocean. Wild Atlantic salmon populations in New England are critically endangered and protected - if you catch one, it must be released immediately. The fish has deep cultural significance for indigenous peoples and was once so abundant that colonial laws prohibited feeding it to servants more than three times per week.
compareHints: Atlantic salmon differ from their closest New England relative, the brown trout, by having a more torpedo-shaped body built for ocean swimming versus the brown trout's more robust, river-adapted form. Atlantic salmon also have fewer and larger spots that disappear in adults, while brown trout keep their distinctive spotted pattern throughout life and have a more golden-brown coloration even when not spawning.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Brown trout differ from their closest relative, Atlantic salmon, by having more spots, a deeper body profile, and staying in freshwater year-round rather than migrating to sea.
